body.hook: Your final Outdoor Ed project brings everything together: an environmental need, a community partner, a plan you design and lead yourselves. Great projects start with a clear problem and a realistic design.

study.title: Design a Project
study.question: How do we design a stewardship project that makes a real difference?
study.passage:
Design steps (written for this lesson):
1. Needs assessment: choose a need from your research or community: e.g. a creek bank eroding in a local park; no recycling or composting at an event; lack of pollinator habitat; heavy litter at a bus stop; idling at school pick-up. Gather evidence: photos, counts, a short survey.
2. Partners: who already works on this? (city, stewardship group, school council, local business).
3. Goals: outputs (e.g. 150 shrubs planted) and outcomes (e.g. reduced erosion measured by photo points; 30% less idling).
4. Plan: tasks, roles, materials, budget, risks and controls, permissions.
5. Timeline: Gantt chart over 4–6 weeks.
6. Communication: how will you involve the community?
7. Proposal (1–2 pages) to the teacher and partner: need and evidence, goals, plan, timeline, budget, how success will be measured.
Peer review: another group checks: Is the need clear? Are goals measurable? Is it realistic?
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.

Plan tasks, budget and a Gantt chart
discussion: What evidence shows the need is real?

study.product: Write a 1–2 page project proposal with evidence of need, partners, measurable goals, a Gantt chart, budget and success measures.

body.hook: Now you lead. Projects rarely go exactly to plan: volunteers cancel, rain falls, supplies arrive late. Strong project leaders communicate, adapt and keep the team moving.

study.title: Leading the Project
study.question: How do we lead a project through to completion?
study.passage:
Leadership routines (written for this lesson):
Weekly stand-up (5 minutes): each member says what they did, what they'll do next and any blockers.
Task board: columns To do / Doing / Done, updated every class.
Delegation: match tasks to strengths; every member has a clear role and deadline.
Communication: email updates to the partner (through the teacher), posters or announcements to involve the school, social media posts by the school with permission.
Advocacy: a short pitch to the school council or an assembly to recruit volunteers or support.
Contingency plans: rain date; backup volunteers; alternative supplier; a scaled-down version if time runs short.
Problem-solving steps: define the problem, list options, choose, act, check.
Log: keep a project journal with dates, decisions, photos and data.

body.hook: The project is done, but the job isn't finished until you know what changed and you've told people about it. Evaluation and sharing turn one project into inspiration for many more.

study.title: Evaluate and Share
study.question: What did our project achieve, and how do we share it?
study.passage:
Evaluation and sharing (written for this lesson):
1. Outputs: count what was produced (shrubs planted, kilograms of waste diverted, posters, volunteers, hours).
2. Outcomes: compare indicators with the baseline (e.g. idling cars 42 → 25; erosion photo points; survey of student awareness before and after). Calculate percentage change.
3. Partner feedback: a short interview or survey.
4. Lessons learned: what worked, what didn't, what we'd change.
5. Legacy: who will continue it? Hand over a care plan or guide.
6. Showcase: a display board or digital presentation for a community showcase (families, partners, school council, local officials invited): need, action, results, photos, thanks.
7. Personal reflection (one page): how your thinking about the environment, community and your own leadership has changed through Outdoor Ed.
